references.text: The older son's complaint that he has served his father for many years without receiving a reward reflects a legalistic attitude. He views his relationship with his father as service based on duty rather than love—an attitude that characterized the Pharisees and scribes whom Jesus addressed in this parable ([ref:Luk 15:2|Luke 15:2]).

The Pharisee in the temple boasts of his own righteousness in a similar way to the older son—both emphasize their own obedience and service as grounds for deserving God's favor ([ref:Luk 18:11-12|Luke 18:11-12]).

The workers who had labored all day complained that those who came late received the same pay—the same attitude of self-righteousness and envy shown by the older son ([ref:Matt 20:11-12|Matthew 20:11-12]).

Israel pursued a law of righteousness but did not attain it because they sought it through works rather than faith—parallel to the older son's attitude that his service should earn him merit ([ref:Rom 9:31-32|Romans 9:31-32]).
The Jews' claim that they had never been anyone's slaves and always stood in right relationship with God recalls the older son's assertion of his own faithful service ([ref:Joh 8:33|John 8:33]).

Jesus says there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance—something that directly challenges the older son's self-understanding ([ref:Luk 15:7|Luke 15:7]).

Jonah became angry when God showed mercy to Nineveh, just as the older son became angry at his father's mercy toward his younger brother. Both reacted with wrath over God's compassion toward the unworthy ([ref:Jona 4:1-2|Jonah 4:1-2]).

The Mosaic law's provision for the firstborn's right to a double portion forms the background for the older son's expectation of being rewarded for his faithfulness and service ([ref:5 Mos 21:17|Deuteronomy 21:17]).

Paul's allegory of Hagar and Sarah illustrates the contrast between slavery under the law and freedom in grace—the older son describes himself with the words "δουλεύω σοι" (I serve as a slave to you), revealing that he experienced his relationship with his father as slavery rather than sonship ([ref:Gal 4:24-25|Galatians 4:24-25]).
